title: THE DISEASE THAT BLINDED SAMSON
paragraphs:
THE DISEASE THAT BLINDED SAMSON
It Was Never His Eyes That Failed First—It Was His Heart
There are tragedies that happen in a moment.
And then there are tragedies that happen so slowly that nobody notices until everything is gone.
Samson's story belongs to the second kind.
Most people remember the ending.
They remember the giant warrior grinding grain in darkness. They remember the chains. They remember the humiliation. They remember the moment the Philistines gouged out his eyes.
But by the time Samson lost his physical sight, he had already been blind for years.
The disease that destroyed Samson was not found in his eyes.
It was found in his heart.
And if we are honest, many of us are fighting the same disease right now.
The story begins with a man chosen by God before he was even born.
An angel appeared to Samson's mother and declared that the child would be set apart for God's purposes (Judges 13:5).
From the beginning, Samson's life carried divine purpose.
He was not ordinary.
He was called.
Empowered.
Anointed.
Marked by heaven.
Yet one of the most terrifying truths in Scripture is that calling does not automatically produce obedience.
Giftedness is not holiness.
Power is not intimacy.
Anointing is not surrender.
Many people today possess incredible talents while secretly drifting away from God.
Samson became living proof that a person can operate in supernatural strength while becoming spiritually weak.
The disease began subtly.
Like most spiritual diseases do.
Judges 14:1 records a seemingly harmless observation:
"I saw a woman in Timnah."
That sentence appears innocent.
But hidden inside it is the beginning of destruction.
Samson saw.
Then desired.
Then demanded.
The Hebrew pattern echoes a much older tragedy.
In Genesis 3:6 Eve "saw" the fruit.
In Joshua 7:21 Achan "saw" the treasure.
In 2 Samuel 11:2 David "saw" Bathsheba.
Sin often begins with misplaced vision.
The eyes become fixed on something God never intended to possess the heart.
What Samson saw with his eyes eventually controlled his soul.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly warn against this danger.
The heart follows what the eyes continually feed upon.
What you repeatedly gaze at eventually becomes what you worship.
Samson did not fall because he lacked strength.
He fell because he lacked self-government.
The strongest man in Israel was powerless over his own desires.
And that is still one of Satan's favorite strategies.
Not to remove your gifts.
Not to remove your opportunities.
Not to remove your calling.
But to convince you that private compromise will never affect public purpose.
The enemy rarely destroys a person in a single battle.
He wins through gradual surrender.
A little compromise.
A little secrecy.
A little rationalization.
A little pride.
Until eventually the soul becomes numb.
The Bible describes Samson repeatedly moving closer and closer to what God had forbidden.
Every compromise made the next compromise easier.
Every act of disobedience became preparation for greater disobedience.
Sin never remains where it begins.
It always grows.
Always spreads.
Always demands more.
The ancient Greek word often used in the New Testament for sin is ἁμαρτία (hamartia), meaning "missing the mark."
The tragedy of Samson is not merely that he sinned.
The tragedy is that he continually missed the purpose for which God created him.
Many believers today are not abandoning God outright.
They are simply drifting.
Missing the mark.
Living beneath their calling.
Settling for lesser things.
Losing sensitivity to the Spirit one compromise at a time.
Then Delilah entered the story.
Her name has become synonymous with betrayal.
But Samson's greatest problem was never Delilah.
It was Samson.
Delilah simply exposed what already existed inside him.
Judges 16 reveals one of the most heartbreaking moments in all Scripture.
After repeatedly playing games with temptation, Samson finally reveals the secret connected to his Nazarite vow.
Then comes the verse that should terrify every believer.
"He did not know that the LORD had left him."
(Judges 16:20)
Read that again.
He did not know.
No alarm sounded.
No lightning struck.
No immediate catastrophe occurred.
He simply reached a moment where God's presence had withdrawn and he was unaware.
That is the frightening reality of spiritual blindness.
The person suffering from it often cannot see it.
The Hebrew word for "know" here implies perception and awareness.
Samson had become spiritually numb.
His heart had lost sensitivity.
The danger was not merely that God had departed.
The danger was that Samson no longer noticed.
Many people fear persecution.
Many fear suffering.
Many fear hardship.
But perhaps the greater danger is becoming comfortable while drifting away from intimacy with God.
To lose awareness of His presence.
To become accustomed to spiritual distance.
To normalize compromise.
To stop grieving what once broke your heart.
That is blindness.
And eventually the blindness inside became blindness outside.
The Philistines seized Samson.
The man who once terrified armies became a public spectacle.
The warrior became a prisoner.
The judge became entertainment.
The eyes that wandered where they should not wander were finally removed altogether.
Scripture says:
"The Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes."
(Judges 16:21)
What a devastating picture.
The very thing that repeatedly led Samson astray became the object of judgment.
Yet this is not where the story ends.
Because God specializes in writing redemption into ruined stories.
This is why Samson's account belongs perfectly within the theme:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The Gospel is not merely the story of people who got things right.
It is the story of God pursuing people who got everything wrong.
At the lowest point of Samson's life, a remarkable sentence appears:
"But the hair of his head began to grow again."
(Judges 16:22)
At first glance it seems insignificant.
Yet spiritually it is profound.
Hope was growing.
Grace was growing.
Restoration was growing.
God was not finished.
The world saw a defeated man.
God saw a redeemed future.
That is the message of the Gospel.
Peter denied Christ.
David committed adultery.
Moses murdered.
Paul persecuted believers.
Yet grace rewrote their stories.
The Greek word χάρις (charis), translated "grace," means undeserved favor freely given.
Grace is not God pretending sin never happened.
Grace is God accomplishing redemption despite what happened.
Grace is not earned.
Grace is received.
This reaches its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
The One Samson ultimately points toward.
Where Samson failed temptation, Jesus overcame it.
Where Samson served himself, Jesus served others.
Where Samson's strength diminished, Christ endured to the end.
Where Samson's life was marked by compromise, Jesus lived in perfect obedience.
And unlike Samson, Jesus willingly allowed Himself to be bound so sinners could be set free.
Isaiah prophesied concerning Christ:
"He was pierced for our transgressions; He was crushed for our iniquities."
(Isaiah 53:5)
At Calvary, Jesus carried the blindness of humanity.
The sin.
The rebellion.
The pride.
The compromise.
The wandering hearts.
The hidden failures.
The secret addictions.
The shame nobody else knows.
He carried them all.
And through His resurrection He offers something Samson desperately needed.
A new heart.
A restored vision.
A redeemed future.
Perhaps as you read this, you recognize Samson's disease inside yourself.
Maybe nobody else sees it.
Maybe your reputation remains intact.
Maybe your ministry still functions.
Maybe your career still succeeds.
Maybe your family thinks everything is fine.
But deep down you know your heart has drifted.
You know compromise has become comfortable.
You know intimacy with God has weakened.
You know your spiritual eyesight is fading.
If so, hear this carefully:
The same God who restored Samson still restores people today.
Your failure is not final.
Your shame is not the end.
Your compromise does not have the last word.
Jesus does.
Repentance is not punishment.
It is an invitation home.
The Aramaic expression ܐܒܐ (Abba), echoed in the New Testament, means "Father."
Not distant ruler.
Not reluctant judge.
Father.
The God who welcomes prodigals.
The God who restores the broken.
The God who turns scandals into testimonies.
The God who rewrites everything through Christ.
Let that be your prayer.
Let that be your confession.
Let that be your beginning.
Not to shame them. Not to embarrass them. But because eternity matters more than comfort.
You may be surprised how many brothers and sisters stand beside you.
Because sometimes the greatest miracle is not that God restores your strength.
It is that He restores your sight.
And once Christ opens your eyes, you can never see your old life the same way again.
The eyes Samson lost were not the greatest tragedy.
The greatest tragedy would have been remaining blind to the grace that was still reaching for him.
